ict-123/equations-and-math/laws/kirchhof.description:
Kirchhoff's current law
Total current going into a junction = the total amount going out
I = I1 + I2 +…
Kirchhoff's voltage law
Kirchhoff's voltage law states that, given any two specific points on a circuit at a particular time, the difference in voltage between the two points (known as the voltage drop) is the same no matter what pathway you take to get there.

#Cleanup-OldFiles.ps1
#Author Skulky Tim
#modifyed by Ryder Fryling
#Created February 27, 2019
#Last Modified mar 14, 2026 #Rationale and Synopsis
#The intention is to locate all the files not used within a specified date in a current directory.
#Once the files are found, user should be given the chance to delete them.
#Current status: Kind of sort of halfish done, but execution not working as expected
#It would also be nice if user could select how old the files should be (e.g. older than 30 days, 10 days, 60 days, etc.) #Variables
$days = Read-Host "enter how many days ago you would like to search" $filepath = (Get-Location)
$olderthandate = (Get-Date).AddDays(-$days) #Execution #creates the table Get-ChildItem -Path $filepath -Recurse | Where-Object {$_.LastWriteTime -le $olderthandate} |
Format-Table -Property Name,LastWriteTime #decision to delete the files if ((Read-Host "delete the Files?") -contains "yes" -or "y") { #gets the files and deletes them Get-ChildItem -Path $filepath -Recurse | Where-Object {$_.LastWriteTime -le $olderthandate} | remove-item -WhatIf }else{ #seccond option saying the files wernt deleted Write-Host "the files wre not deleted" } <# .SYNOPSIS The intention is to locate all the files not used within a specified date in a current directory. .DESCRIPTION The intention is to locate all the files not used within a specified date in a current directory. Once the files are found, user should be given the chance to delete them. .SYNOPSIS this script gatheres information from a inputted list of computers and compiles the collected information in a CSV file. .DESCRIPTION
this script gatheres information from a inputted list of computers and compiles the collected information in a CSV file. it will only create the file when a location is given specifying where the file is to be located. .PARAMETER InfoClass
this is the type of information that is to be gethered. only one type can be gathered at a time .PARAMETER Device
you can input a list of devices to gether information from. this has to be a string. .PARAMETER OutFile_Path
This parameter specifyes the location of where the CSV file is to be created. it is also the switch for the creation of a CSV file. .EXAMPLE
PS C:\Users\bob\Desktop> .\Get-CIMComputerInfo.ps1 -Device DESKTOP-GQ327M5,LocalHost -InfoClass LogicalDisk -OutFile_Path .\ Win32_LogicalDisk: C: (DeviceID = "C:") Win32_LogicalDisk: D: (DeviceID = "D:") DeviceID DriveType ProviderName VolumeName Size FreeSpace PSComputerName -------- --------- ------------ ---------- ---- --------- -------------- C: 3 135406809088 109951479808 DESKTOP-GQ327M5
D: 5 CPBA_X64FRE_EN-US_DV9 6969382912 0 DESKTOP-GQ327M5
C: 3 135406809088 109951479808 LocalHost D: 5 CPBA_X64FRE_EN-US_DV9 6969382912 0 LocalHost LastWriteTime : 3/29/2026 11:51:01 PM
Length : 0
Name : WS-Info-CIM-LogicalDisk-2026-51-29.csv .EXAMPLE

----------------- ------------ ---- ------------ ------- --------------
Hyper-V UEFI Release v4.1 Microsoft Corporation Hyper-V UEFI Release v4.1 8546-1777-1739-7800-3950-9116-75 VRTUAL - 1 LocalHost #>
param( [ValidateSet("BIOS", "OS", "Service", "LogicalDisk")] [string] $InfoClass = "LogicalDisk", [array] $Device = "LocalHost", [parameter(Mandatory = $false)] [string] $OutFile_Path, [parameter(Mandatory = $false)] [switch] $Start_RM ) #matches the class to the inputed parameter if ($InfoClass -eq "BIOS") { $InfoClass_var = "CIM_BIOSElement" } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "OS"){ $InfoClass_var = "CIM_OperatingSystem" } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "Service"){ $InfoClass_var = "CIM_Service" } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "LogicalDisk"){ $InfoClass_var = "CIM_LogicalDisk"} #starts WinRM on the local host if needed if ($Start_RM){ Start-Service -Name WinRM } #creates terminal output $Device | ForEach-Object { Get-CimInstance -ComputerName $_ -ClassName $InfoClass_var |Format-Table -AutoSize -Wrap

#Get-ServiceHealthReport.ps1
#Author: Ryder Fryling #Created: 2026/03/22
#Version 1.0
#Updated: N/A
#Description: This script Audits Windows services by status, startup type, and service account. <#
.SYNOPSIS Audits Windows services by status, startup type, and service account. .DESCRIPTION Queries Windows services using Get-Service and Get-CimInstance, then filters and reports based on the specified criteria. Useful for identifying stopped auto-start services, services running under non-standard accounts, or summarizing overall service health. .PARAMETER Status Filter services by status. Valid values: Running, Stopped, All. Defaults to All. .PARAMETER StartupType Filter by startup type. Valid values: Automatic, Manual, Disabled, All. Defaults to All. .PARAMETER AccountFilter If specified, shows only services running under this account name (partial match). For example, "LocalSystem" or "Network". .PARAMETER SortBy Property to sort results by. Valid values: Name, Status, StartType. Defaults to Name. .EXAMPLE .\Get-ServiceHealthReport.ps1 Lists all services sorted by name. .EXAMPLE .\Get-ServiceHealthReport.ps1 -Status Stopped -StartupType Automatic Shows only stopped services that are configured to start automatically (potential problems that need attention). .EXAMPLE .\Get-ServiceHealthReport.ps1 -AccountFilter "LocalSystem" -SortBy Status Shows services running as LocalSystem, sorted by their current status.
#>
param( [validateSet("Running", "Stopped", "All")] [string]$Status = "All", [validateSet("Automatic", "Manual", "Disabled", "Auto", "All")] [string]$StartupType = "All", [Parameter(Mandatory = $False)] [string]$AccountFilter, [validateSet("Name", "Status", "StartType", "StartMode", "State")] [string]$SortBy = "Name" ) #gets the services $services = Get-CimInstance -ClassName Win32_Service #sorts them by status
if ($Status -ne "All") { $services = $services | Where-Object { $_.State -eq $Status } } #sorts them by start type if ($StartupType -ne "All") { $services = $services | Where-Object { $_.StartMode -eq $StartupType } } #filters the accounts to best match user input if ($AccountFilter) { $services = $services | Where-Object { $_.StartName -like "*$AccountFilter*" } } #formats the $SortBy to be valid input options if ($SortBy -eq "Status") { $SortBy = "State" } elseif ($SortBy -eq "StartType") { $SortBy = "StartMode" } #sorts the data then makes the table and formats it $services | Sort-Object -Property $SortBy | ForEach-Object { [PSCustomObject]@{ Name = $_.Name DisplayName = $_.DisplayName Status = $_.State StartType = $_.StartMode Account = $_.StartName } } | Format-Table -Property Name,Status,StartType,Account,DisplayName -AutoSize -Wrap

#Get-WMIComputerInfo.ps1
#Author: Ryder Fryling #Created: 2026/03/28
#Version 1.0
#Updated: N/A
#Description: this script gathers diffrent WMI info from a computer specifyed by the user <#
.SYNOPSIS this script gathers diffrent WMI info from a computer specifyed by the user .DESCRIPTION this script gathers diffrent WMI info from a computer specifyed by the user. i can also creat a file in a specifyed location if needed. it will also format some of the data. .PARAMETERInfoClass
this is the type of WMI information being collected .PARAMETER Device the device that the information is being collected from .PARAMETER OutFile_Path
the swithc for creating a file with the information as well as the path of its location. .EXAMPLE PS C:\Users\bob\Desktop> .\Get-WMIComputerInfo.ps1 -InfoClass LogicalDisk -Device DESKTOP-GQ327M5 DeviceID DriveType ProviderName FreeSpace Size VolumeName -------- --------- ------------ --------- ---- ---------- C: 3 109947891712 135406809088 D: 5 0 6969382912 CPBA_X64FRE_EN-US_DV9 .EXAMPLE
PS C:\Users\bob\Desktop> .\Get-WMIComputerInfo.ps1 -OutFile_Path .\ SMBIOSBIOSVersion Manufacturer Name SerialNumber Version ----------------- ------------ ---- ------------ ------- Hyper-V UEFI Release v4.1 Microsoft Corporation Hyper-V UEFI Release v4.1 8546-1777-1739-7800-3950-9116-75 VRTUAL - 1 #>
param( [ValidateSet("BIOS", "OS", "Service", "LogicalDisk")] [string] $InfoClass = "BIOS", [string] $Device = "LocalHost", [parameter(Mandatory = $false)] [string] $OutFile_Path )
#sets the variable for the type of data being collected if ($InfoClass -eq "BIOS") { $InfoClass_var = "Win32_Bios" } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "OS"){ $InfoClass_var = "Win32_OperatingSystem" } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "Service"){ $InfoClass_var = "Win32_Service" } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "LogicalDisk"){ $InfoClass_var = "Win32_LogicalDisk" } #creates the formatting for the teble and data
if ($InfoClass -eq "BIOS"){ $Table_Data = Select-Object -Property SMBIOSBIOSVersion,Name,Version,SerialNumber,Manufacturer } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "OS"){ $Table_Data = Select-Object -Property SystemDirectory,Organization,BuildNumber,SerialNumber,Version } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "Service"){ $Table_Data = Select-Object -Property Name,ProccessID,StartMode,State } elseif ($InfoClass -eq "LogicalDisk"){ $Table_Data = Select-Object -Property DeviceID,@{name='FreeSpace';expression={[Math]::Round($_.FreeSpace / 1MB, 3)}}, @{name='Size';expression={[math]::Round($_.Size / 1GB, 3)}}, @{name='%Free';expression={[Math]::Round($_.FreeSpace / $_.Size * 100, 3)}} } #collects info $Device_Data = Get-WmiObject -Class $InfoClass_var -ComputerName $Device |Select-Object $Table_Data #creates file name and full path
$File_Name = "$($Device)-$($InfoClass)-$(Get-Date -Format yyyy-mm-dd).csv"
$OutFile_Path_compleate = $OutFile_Path + "\" + $File_Name #creates file if specifyed if ($OutFile_Path) { Get-WmiObject -Class $InfoClass_var -ComputerName $Device |Select-Object $Table_Data |Export-Csv -Path $OutFile_Path_compleate } #prints data to the terminal $Device_Data |Format-Table -AutoSize -Wrap

# date created: 05/03/2026
# date modified: 16/03/2026
# author: Erik Bjerstedt
#
# Synopsis: automatically creates AD users on the system from a CSV file
#
# Warning: This script assumes that your OU structure and naming (including capitalization) is identical to the project's ADDS diagram.
# Before running, verify that your OUs are structured correctly.
#
# Citations:
# ICT 128 Lab 07 - Full lab.pdf - Phase 3 used as reference # defining default password
$defaultPass = ConvertTo-SecureString "S@lta5002!" -AsPlainText -Force # importing the csv
$userList = Import-Csv -Path (Read-Host "Enter your CSV file's full path")
Write-Host "$($userList.Count) users loaded from CSV." # processing CSV users
foreach ($user in $userList) { # getting name $fName = $user.'First Name'.Trim() $lName = $user.'Last Name'.Trim() $fullName = "$fName.$lName" # building SAM and UPN $sam = ($fullName -replace '[^a-zA-Z0-9]', '').ToLower() $upn = "$sam@atlas.com" # building path $subDept = $user.Subdepartment $title = $user.Title if ($subDept.Length -gt 5) {$subDept = $subDept.Substring(0, 5)} forEach ($OU in (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -like "*"})) { if ($title.Contains("Owner")) { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -eq "Owners"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($title.Contains("VP")) { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -eq "VPs"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($title.Contains("Operations")) { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -like "Operations*"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($title -ceq "CIO") { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -eq "C-Suite"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($subDept -eq "Accou") { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -eq "Finance"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($SubDept -eq ("Administration")) { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -eq "Administration"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($title.Contains("Administrator")) { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -like "IT-Admin*"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($title.Contains("Technician")) { $OUPath = (Get-ADOrganizationalUnit -Filter {Name -eq "IT-Staff"}).DistinguishedName break } elseif ($OU.Name.Contains($subDept)) { $OUPath = $OU.DistinguishedName break } } # creating ADuser New-ADUser ` -GivenName $fName ` -Surname $lName ` -Name $fullName ` -DisplayName "$fName $lName" ` -SamAccountName $sam ` -UserPrincipalName $upn ` -Department $user.Department ` -Title $user.Title ` -AccountPassword $defaultPass ` -EmployeeID $user.'Employee ID' ` -Office $user.'Office Location' ` -OfficePhone $user.'Office Local Phone' ` -EmailAddress $upn ` -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true ` -Enabled $true ` -Path "$OUPath" # confirming creation $created = Get-ADUser -Identity $sam -Properties Enabled -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue if ($created){ # if user creation succeeds Write-Host "$sam successfully created (Enabled: $($created.Enabled))" -ForegroundColor Green Write-Host " SubDepartment: $($subDept), OU: $($OUPath)" } else { # if user creation fails Write-Host "Failed: $sam" -ForegroundColor Red } #reseting path $OUPath = ""
} # finish message
Write-Host "`nImport complete. $($userList.Count) users processed."

ict-128/scripting/example-scripts/kill-p.description:
#Kill-Process.ps1
#Author Skulky Tim
#modifyed by Ryder Fryling
#Created February 27, 2019
#Last Modified mar 14, 2026 #Rationale and Synopsis
#The intention of the script is to allow the user to select a running process from a list and pretend kill it. #Current status - loop works, needs followup #Variables
#collects input for which pocess we want
$letter = Read-Host "Let's pretend to kill a process.`n`nPlease enter a letter of the alphabet"
#gets the processes and prepairs them for output
$array = (Get-Process -Name $letter*)
$counter = 1 #Execution #output for the head of the table Write-Host "These are the current running processes starting with the letter $letter`:" # creates a table of the collected processes ForEach ($process in $array)
{
Write-Output "[$counter] $($process.name)"
$counter++
} #Lets the user choose a process, then stop it with a -WhatIf
$chosen = Read-Host "choose a process tro pretend kill (enter the number)" Stop-Process -Name ($array[($chosen -1)]).Name -WhatIf <# .SYNOPSIS The intention of the script is to allow the user to select a running process from a list and pretend kill it. .DESCRIPTION the script allows the user to select a bunch of processes statrting with a letter. it creates a list from a inputted letter then we can select a process from that list and see what could happen if we killed it #>

#Reset-ADUserPassword.ps1
#Your Name Here
#modifyed by Ryder Fryling
#Created March 6, 2019
#Last Modified mar 14, 2026 #Synopsis
#This script resets a given AD user's password and forces a password change at next logon.
#Script could be modified to allow for a string of users to reset multiple users at once. #Set Variables
Get-ADUser -Filter * | Format-Table -Property name
$user = ""
$ulist = @() #creates the array of users whos passwords are to be reset
while ($user -ne "next") { $user = Read-Host "Enter logon name of the user for whom you'd like to reset the password (type `'next`' to continue)" #adds user to the array unless the input is equal to exit if ($user -ne "next") { $ulist += "$user" } } #Execution #loop to reset the passwords $ulist | foreach { Set-ADUser -Identity $_ -ChangePasswordAtLogon $true -WhatIf } <# .SYNOPSIS This script resets a given AD user's password and forces a password change at next logon. .DESCRIPTION the script allow the user to input multiple users to reset the password for. they can continue by typing exit. the script will then create a array and cycle through it to reset the passwords of the inputted users. #>

WQL (WMI Query Language) is a read-only query language for WMI, modelled on SQL. ict-128/windows-info/cim-vs-wmi-vs-nativ.title: CIM vs WMI vs Native PS CMDlets
ict-128/windows-info/cim-vs-wmi-vs-nativ.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-128/windows-info/cim-vs-wmi-vs-nativ.description: It is a Windows service that exposes hardware, operating system components, and software as structured objects that PowerShell (and other tools) can query. WMI has been built into Windows since Windows 2000. WMI is the windows version of CMI. it is no longer being developed or supported it is being phased out and is not in PS 7 It is a vendor-neutral standard published by the Distributed Management Task Force (DMTF) that defines how system components should be described as objects. WMI is Microsoft's Windows-specific implementation of this standard. the universal version of WMI used to get info about the OS is not available on windows 7 or older you will need to use WMI on those OS's cannot be piped ( | ) Namespaces are the top-level containers. They group related classes together. The most important namespace for network and system administration is root\CIMV2. PowerShell uses this namespace by default when you run Get-CimInstance without specifying one.Other namespaces serve specialised purposes: root\SecurityCenter2: antivirus and firewall product information root\WMI: hardware performance data root\MicrosoftDNS: DNS server management (on DNS servers only) My summery This is like the Directory/folder that the data is located in. Classes define the structure of a type of system component. A class lists all the properties that objects of that type have, along with their data types. Class names follow a convention: Win32_*: provided by the Win32 provider; covers OS, hardware, and networking CIM_*: base classes from the CIM standard; Win32 classes inherit from these __* (double underscore): WMI system classes, metadata about WMI itself My Summery this is the type/format of where the data comes from Instances are the actual data objects, one instance per real component matching the class template. The class Win32_NetworkAdapter defines what properties a network adapter object has; each installed adapter (physical and virtual) is a separate instance of that class.Note Some classes always return exactly one instance (Win32_OperatingSystem) there is only one operating system. Others return many (Win32_NetworkAdapter) one per adapter. Knowing which to expect is part of reading query output correctly.

ict-137/general-info/boot-sequence.html.description:
POST - power on self test - stored in ROM
loads the boot loader software
Boot loader initalizes the CPU
Boot loader initializes the FLASH file system
Bootloader loads the OS
POST is layer 1 - anything with the physical components
Processing (CPU)
Memory (RAM)
Storage (HDD/SSD)
Networking (sometimes optional, NIC) Temp RAM
This is volatile - wont survive a shutdown
Running config is saved in RAM  Permanent SSD
HDD
Isn't volatile - will survive a shutdown
Know sometimes as ROM - POST is here
FLASH is where OS/configs/VLAN database are stored  POST is layer 1 - anything with the physical components
LEDs are layer 1
Frames layer 2 Runts = frame<64 bytes
Giant = frame > 1518 bytes

ict-137/routing/concepts/ospfv2-concept..icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-137/routing/concepts/ospfv2-concept..description:
a large area dynamic routing protocol. Elect a Designated Router (DR) Elect Backup Designated Router (BDR) All other routers are Drothers highest score wins order of importance Interface Priority Router ID Loopback address Active IP address on any interface on the router NOTE: Interface Priority We don’t change the interface priority very often. the DR is responsible for collecting and distributing all of the Link State Advertisements (LSAs) within the area. it stores these in a database which it then is responsible for sending to all of the Drothers. the DR uses the multicast address 224.0.0.5 for all OSPF routers. the BDR maintains a close relationship with the DR and keeps a backup of all relationships and the database. in the event that the DR is no longer active it assumes the role of DR. its a read only version of the Link State Database all routers or layer 3 switches in an area that are neither a DR or a BDR. use the multicast address 224.0.0.6 to send messages to the DR and BDR also see WCM - Wild Card Mask

ict-211/hyper-v-and-hypervisors.html.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-211/hyper-v-and-hypervisors.html.description:
. A Hypervisor is the software layer on a physical host that coordinates virtual machines. A Hypervisor manages virtual machines and is responsible for allocating resources to each virtual machine. The Hypervisor is ultimately what makes virtualization possible. There are two types of Hypervisor: Type 1 and Type 2 Also known as the "Bare Metal Hypervisor" Type 1 Hypervisor is installed directly on the physical host Has direct access to the physical resources of the physical host which then allocates the available resources to the virtual machines Hypervisor loads (boots) first, before the Operating System Administrators have the ability to create clusters with many Type 1 Hypervisors (but not all) Also known as "Hosted Hypervisor" Type 2 Hypervisor is installed on top of the host Operating System (ie Windows 10) The host Operating System manages the hardware resources The Type 2 Hypervisor requests the resources from the Operating System Type 2 Hypervisors do not support clustering Type 1 Hypervisors have better performance compared to Type 2 Type 1 Hypervisors have direct access to hardware resources! Type 2 Hypervisors need to request resources from the OS first, the OS then accesses the hardware resources Hyper-V is Type 1
Hyper-V is a Type 1 Hypervisor! Can be confusing because on Windows 10 / 11 it's a Feature that's enabled from the Control Panel Can be confusing because on Server 2016/2019/2022 it's enabled as a Server Role Hyper-V Manager "appears" to look like an application, but this is what an administrator uses to create/manage VMs Hyper-V is the Virtual Machine Manager When Creating New VM’s When creating New Server VM’s use datacenter not standard. Datacenter supports clusters. For exporting and importing VMs from your home computer to the ICT Lab environment create a private vSwitch named "Private Virtual Switch" vSwitch names The name of the vSwitch is case sensitive. Your computer with Hyper-V already has the "Default Switch" configured To complete a successful Export (Copy/Backup) of a VM using Hyper-V Manager: Ensure the VM is shut down / turned off Remove the DVD / CD Drive from the VM Export the VM to the desired location using Hyper-V Manager by clicking Export ... (ie to an External Hard Drive - SSD) There are 3 Types of Imports when using Hyper-V Manager This type of import allows you to import, or "register," a VM where the files and VHD of the VM are already moved to the host You can perform this import when the files are already moved to the new host (ie VM files are cut and pasted from an SSD to a host computer prior to starting the Import process) This import will maintain the same unique ID this if faster then restore since it doesn't need to move a bunch of files. less work for hyper-v. This type of import allows you to import by copying the files and VHD of the VM are from one location to another This import will copy the VM files to a new host, the original files will remain in-tact on the original source (ie VM files saved on an SSD) The original exported files remain unchanged and can be reused for future imports This import will also maintain the same unique ID of the VM This type of import allows you to create "templates" of VMs This type of import can create multiple instances of the same VM on the same host This import will create a new ID for each VM You will not need to use this type of import for this course!

ict-211/os-and-protection-rings.html.description: Protection Rings is a type of Architecture for Operating Systems The higher the ring, the less privilege it has to access tasks and functions in the lower levels Most Operating Systems use Ring 0, the Kernel, a program layer that communicates, translates instructions and schedules hardware resources (CPU, Memory, Storage, etc) Ring 3 is also known as the "User Space," where users interact with the software of the computer system Virtualization allows hypervisors to access Ring O, the Kernel, directly for computation and instructions Hyper-V can be considered Ring -1. Allows for best performance and for the hypervisor to manage, instruct and schedule the resources

ict-211/virtual-switches.html.description:
Virtual Switches Do not change the virtual switches on the lab machines, only on nested VM’s may you change them. Private Virtual Switches only establish connectivity between virtual machines within a host There is no external connectivity outside of the host External Virtual Switches connect to a network interface card (NIC) on the host essentially “takes over” that NIC Establishes connectivity between virtual machines and intermediary devices (ie physical router) connected to the host Can also establish connectivity between virtual machines and other physical host
Hypervisors can also provide virtual machines with immediate connectivity to the internet This is known as the "Default Switch" on Windows 11. This is not included with Server! This type of virtual switch essentially makes the host a multi-function routing device Designed to provide immediate internet connectivity to VMs The host provides DHCP and NAT services to VMs with the Default Switch However, the VMs do not have connectivity to the physical host
Internal Virtual Switches can establish connectivity between virtual machines and the physical host Internal Virtual Switches are rarely used

ict-212/definitions/ethical-hacking.html.title: Ethical hacking
ict-212/definitions/ethical-hacking.html.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-212/definitions/ethical-hacking.html.description:
An ethical hacker uses hacking knowledge and techniques, which is the same as those used by malicious hacker, with authorization to identify vulnerabilities and improve security.
Activities may include vulnerability research and assessment, penetration testing, network testing, web application testing and wireless testing.
Ethical hackers may also assess human and procedural weaknesses when explicitly authorized.
The technical skills can overlap with malicious hacking. However, authorization, scope, intent and professional conduct make the difference.
The main difference Ethical hackers have permission to hack an organization and only go where they have permission to go within that organization. Ethical hacking can discover vulnerabilities before malicious attackers exploit them. It helps validate security controls and identify configuration mistakes. It can demonstrate realistic attack paths and help organizations prioritize remediation. It also supports security improvement, incident preparedness and compliance activities. Golden rule: never test a system unless you have permission.
Obtain clear authorization and understand the agreed scope.
Stay within scope and minimize unnecessary impact or damage.
Protect confidential information discovered during testing.
Document findings accurately and report vulnerabilities responsibly.
Never use discovered information or access for personal benefit.
Important
just because you can doesn't mean you should
. You are authorized to test 192.168.10.20.
. During reconnaissance you discover that 192.168.10.21 appears
vulnerable.
· Can you attack 192.168.10.21?
. No - not unless the additional system is included in the authorized scope.
. Technical ability does not create authorization.

It is intelligence collected and analyzed from publicly available information.· Possible sources: websites, search engines, social media, news, public documents, DNS/domain information, job postings, maps and public code repositories.· In ethical hacking, OSINT can reveal useful information about a target before active testing begins.· Open-source intelligence does not mean open-source software.. Company website -> employee names and organizational information· Employee information -> possible email naming conventions. Job advertisements -> technologies and platforms used by the organization. Domain and DNS information - internet-facing infrastructure· Combined information - better understanding of the potential attack surface· Important: information collection and subsequent testing must still respect authorization and scope.

Otherwise known as a Ethical Hacker.May identify vulnerabilities without authorization, even when the intent is not malicious.Distinction good intention does not automatically make hacking legal or ethical. Cybercriminal - financial gain Hacktivist - political or social motivation Insider - revenge, financial motivation, negligence or accidental actions State-sponsored attacker - espionage, intelligence or national objectives Script kiddie - curiosity, challenge or status, often using existing tools Different threat actors can use similar techniques for very different reasons. Reconnaissance - gather information about the target. Scanning & Enumeration - identify hosts, ports, services, systems, users and potential weaknesses. Gaining Access - exploit a vulnerability, weak credential, misconfiguration or human weakness. Maintaining Access - establish persistence or continued access. Covering Tracks - attempt to hide evidence and avoid detection. ict-212/osint-tools.html.description:
Rather than memorizing tools, start with the information you need. People & organizations - names, roles, contact patterns Domains & infrastructure - WHOIS/RDAP, DNS, certificates Technology - website technologies, public service information Historical information - archived websites and documents Search & discovery - search engines, specialized OSINT indexes A tool is useful only when it answers a reconnaissance question. OSINT Framework organizes many publicly available research tools by category. https://osintframework.com Google dorking uses advanced search operators to narrow search results and locate specific publicly indexed information. It is not "hacking Google"- it uses normal search features in a more precise way. It can help locate particular file types, pages within a domain, text in titles or URLs, and exposed public information. Ethical use still requires attention to authorization, privacy and responsible handling of findings. intitle:”index of /” - shows the file struckture
A search result becomes useful intelligence only after analysis. Ask: Is the information current? Is the source trustworthy? Does another source confirm it? How does it relate to other findings? Is it relevant to the authorized objective? Reconnaissance is not just collecting data - it is connecting and validating information.

ict-212/recconnasance.html.title: Recconnasance
ict-212/recconnasance.html.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-212/recconnasance.html.description: Overview of reconnaissance Passive vs active reconnaissance Ethics, authorization and scope OSINT tools and information sources Search engines and Google dorking WHOIS, Ping and DNS Reconnaissance is the information-gathering phase of an attack or security assessment. The goal is to learn as much as possible about a target before attempting further actions. Information gathered can reveal: people technologies domains systems relationships possible weaknesses. More complete information can help an attacker or ethical hacker plan the next phase more effectively. Reconnaissance reduces uncertainty about the target. It helps build a picture of the target's attack surface. Small pieces of public information can become valuable when combined. Examples: employee names + email format + technology used + domain information. Key idea information itself can become part of an attack path. we may have to think like a threat actor to figure out their way in. Common goals include: Identify the organization and its online presence Discover domains, subdomains and IP information Identify technologies and services in use Learn about employees, roles and contact information Discover relationships with vendors or partners Identify information that may support later scanning, enumeration or social engineering The goals of reconnaissance are not limited to the above - any relevant information that helps us better understand the target can be valuable. Note One of the easiest ways in is social security. Publicly available does not mean unrestricted use is always appropriate. Passive research can still collect personal, sensitive or organizational information. Active reconnaissance may interact with systems and generate traffic. The method, purpose, authorization and scope all matter. An ethical hacker should collect only what is necessary for the authorized objective.

ict-218/day-one-and-two-218.html.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-218/day-one-and-two-218.html.description:
Book Quiz 1 Quiz Date: September 18 (Take home) deadline: September 21, 12 PM Covers: Windows 2025 chapter 1-4, and Security+, chapter 1. By the end of this lecture, students should be able to: Define security controls and explain their purpose. Describe the four categories of security controls. Differentiate between control categories and control types. Explain the six major control types using the PDDCCD framework. Apply security control concepts to real-world cybersecurity scenarios. Identify examples of controls used in organizations. Analyze how multiple controls work together through Defense in Depth have layers to your security Security controls are safeguards or countermeasures that protect an organization’s: Information Systems Networks Facilities Employees The purpose of security controls is to reduce risk by: Preventing attacks Detecting attacks Responding to incidents Recovering from disruption No organization can completely eliminate risk. Threats constantly evolve: Hackers Malware Insider threats disgruntled employee bad software Social engineering attacks Physical theft Organizations implement security controls to minimize the chances of successful attacks and reduce the impact when incidents occur. A common cybersecurity strategy is called Defense in Depth.Defense in Depth means using multiple layers of security controls rather than relying on a single protection mechanism.Imagine a company protecting a file server:If one layer fails, additional layers continue protecting the organizationA user's password is stolen.Without MFA: Attacker logs in immediately. With MFA: If Passwords are compromised. MFA blocks access. The security team receives an alert. One failed control does not necessarily mean a security breach. Security controls are grouped into four major categoriesTechnical controls are implemented through hardware or software systems. They automatically enforce security requirements.Protect digital assets using technology. Firewalls A firewall filters network traffic. Functions: Allows authorized traffic Blocks unauthorized traffic Monitors network communications Example: A firewall blocks incoming traffic from known malicious IP addresses Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) MFA requires multiple forms of verification. Three common factors: Something you know Password Something you have Smartphone Smart card Something you are Fingerprint Facial recognition Example Logging into Microsoft 365 requires: Username Password Approval through Microsoft Authenticator Encryption Encryption converts readable data into ciphertext.
this works hand in hand with the CIA Triad Benefits: Protects confidentiality Prevents unauthorized access Secures sensitive information Examples: HTTPS websites BitLocker drive encryption VPN communications Antivirus and Endpoint Protection Functions: Detect malware Block malicious programs Quarantine infected files Remove threats Real-world Example: Microsoft Defender identifies ransomware activity and isolates the affected device. Managerial controls are administrative processes used to manage security programs.Create security governance and oversight. Security Policies Policies establish management's security expectations. Examples: Password policy Remote work policy Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) Policies tell employees what they can and cannot do. Risk Assessments Organizations must identify: Threats Vulnerabilities Potential impacts Questions include: What can go wrong? How likely is it? What would be the impact? Security Awareness Training Human error remains a major cause of security incidents. Training helps employees: Identify phishing attacks Recognize suspicious behavior Follow security procedures Audits and Compliance Reviews Audits verify: Policies are followed Controls are working Regulatory requirements are met Examples: ISO 27001 audits PCI-DSS assessments Internal security reviews Operational controls are security activities performed by people during daily operations.Ensure security procedures are consistently followed. Account Management Examples: Creating user accounts Disabling terminated employees Reviewing permissions Poor account management frequently leads to unauthorized access. Incident Response When a security incident occurs: • Detect • Analyze • Contain • Eradicate • Recover Organizations develop incident response procedures before an attack occurs. Security Monitoring Security analysts continuously monitor: • Event logs • Security alerts • Network activity Example: Microsoft Sentinel identifying suspicious login activity. User Awareness Programs Employees learn: • Secure password practices • Email security • Social engineering awareness Users become part of the organization's security defense. Physical controls protect facilities, equipment, and personnel.Prevent unauthorized physical access.Locks and Keys Protect: • Server rooms • Data centers • Equipment cabinets Security Guards Provide: • Visible security presence • Access verification • Emergency response CCTV Surveillance Functions: • Monitor activity • Record evidence • Support investigations Fencing and Gates Used to create secure boundaries around facilities. Examples: • Data centers • Power plants • Corporate campuses Mantraps A mantrap is a small, controlled entry area containing two doors. Purpose: • Only one person enters at a time. • Prevents tailgating attacks. Commonly used in: • Data centers • Research laboratories • Government facilitiesCategories tell us what kind of control it is. Types tell us what the control does.Stop attacks before they occur.• MFA • Firewalls • Encryption • Access control lists • Security patchesA firewall blocks malicious traffic before it reaches a server.Discourage of attacks. The control may not stop an attack but makes attackers think twice.• Warning signs • Security guards • Cameras • Alarm systemsCriminals often avoid facilities with visible monitoring systems.Identify attacks that occur or have occurred.• Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) • Security logs • SIEM solutions • CCTV recordingsMicrosoft Sentinel detects repeated failed login attempts and generates an alert.Restore systems after an incident.• Malware removal • Backup restoration • Patch deployment • Disaster recovery plansA company restores encrypted files after a ransomware attack using backups.Provide alternative protection when the preferred control cannot be implemented.• Additional monitoring • VPN-only access • Manual approvalsA legacy application cannot support MFA.• VPN access only • Restricted access hours • Increased monitoringProvide instructions and guidance.• Security policies • Procedures • Standards • Acceptable Use PoliciesA corporate password policy requiring: • Minimum 12 characters • Complexity requirements • Regular reviewsSecurity+ Memory Aid Security controls reduce organizational risk. Defense in Depth uses multiple security layers. Four categories of controls:
Technical
Managerial
Operational
Physical Six common control types:
Preventive
Deterrent
Detective
Corrective
Compensating
Directive One control can belong to multiple control types. Security+ examinations frequently test control categories and PDDCCD classifications

ict-218/mechanisms.html.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-218/mechanisms.html.description: Average data breach cost exceeds $10 million for U.S. organizations. Attackers often remain undetected for months. Most breaches originate from compromised credentials. Social engineering remains one of the most effective attack vectors. Built-in anti-malware and antivirus protection included with Windows Server 2025. Enabled by default. Real-time protection. Virus and threat protection. Automatic updates. Tight integration with Windows. Enable/disable real-time protection. Manage scans. Update threat definitions. Monitor security status. Updating When updating on a server you must evaluate impact and schedule downtime. Enterprise Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) platform. Behavioral analysis Threat detection Incident investigation Automated remediation Centralized management Detects advanced threats. Uses cloud intelligence. Shares threat intelligence across Microsoft customers. A malicious attachment received by one Microsoft customer may be automatically blocked for all others once identified.Attack Surface Reduction (ASR) Blocks risky behaviors such as: Office macros launching scripts Executables from email Suspicious processes Network Protection Uses Microsoft SmartScreen to: Block malicious websites Prevent communication with known attacker infrastructure only in edge - not integrated on other browsers Controlled Folder Access Protects critical files from ransomware encryption.Exploit Protection Provides memory and exploit mitigations against software/ransomware attacks.Host-based firewall protection built into Windows. Control Panel Firewall Windows Security Firewall Settings Windows Defender Firewall with Advanced Security (WFAS) Modern Windows Firewall provides: Stateful inspection Inbound/Outbound rules IPsec integration Connection Security Rules Network firewalls alone are not sufficient. Host-based firewalls provide an additional security layer.Activated when connected to Active Directory.Trusted networks such as home or office.Least trusted network profile.Different security rules can apply automatically based on network location.A laptop may use: • Domain profile at work • Private profile at home • Public profile at an airport Block RDP from external interfaces Allow ICMP (Ping) Restrict traffic to specific subnets Configure inbound/outbound rules Apply firewall rules centrally through Group Policy.Protects: Data at Rest Data in Transit Also See 3 States of Data • BitLocker • EFS • IPsec • Encrypted Virtual NetworksPrevent unauthorized access even if infrastructure or storage systems are compromised.Full disk encryption technology.Benefits Protects: Laptops Servers Virtual Machines Allows virtual machines to: Store encryption keys securely Use BitLocker without physical TPM hardware Must be enabled to use. BitLocker protects data even if virtual hard disks are stolen or copied.Protect Hyper-V virtual machines against host-level attacks. BitLocker encryption Virtual TPM Host Guardian Service integration Useful in multi-tenant or cloud environments where infrastructure administrators must not access guest data. Encrypted File System (EFS) Purpose Encrypts individual files and folders. Requirements • User certificate • PKI infrastructure Limitation Security depends heavily on protection of the user's credentials. Comparison Technology Protects BitLocker Entire drive EFS Selected files/folders IPsec Purpose Encrypts network traffic. Uses • VPN (IKEv2) • DirectAccess • Internal network encryption Policy Types Server Policy Requests encrypted communications. Secure Server Policy Requires encrypted communications. Client Policy Responds to encryption requests. Microsoft Entra Password Protection Purpose Blocks weak and commonly used passwords. Features • Microsoft's global banned password list • Custom banned passwords • Integration with on-premises AD Examples Blocked passwords: • Password • Password123 • P@ssword Security Benefit Reduces credential compromise. Fine-Grained Password Policies (FGPP) Purpose Apply different password policies to different users or groups. Examples Group Password Policy Sales Staff Strong passwords, short expiration Manufacturing Staff Less restrictive requirements Key Components • AD Administrative Center (ADAC) • Password Settings Objects (PSOs) • Precedence values Security Point Supports risk-based security controls. Windows LAPS Purpose Automatically rotates local administrator passwords. Benefits • Unique password per device • Password rotation • Central storage • Protection against Pass-the-Hash attacks Storage Locations • Active Directory • Microsoft Entra Key Commands 1 Update-LapsADSchema 2 Get-LapsADPassword 3 Set-LapsADPasswordExpirationTime One of the most important identity security technologies available today. Microsoft Defender for Identity Evolution ATA → Azure ATP → Defender for Identity Capabilities • Identity threat detection • Behavioral analytics • Lateral movement detection • Pass-the-Ticket detection • Credential theft detection Uses Machine Learning Identifies abnormal user behavior and possible compromises. Security Best Practices Least Privilege Users should not have administrator rights. Separate Administrative Accounts Use: • Standard user account • Administrative account Privileged Access Workstations (PAW) Use separate computers or VMs for administrative functions. Avoid Internet Browsing on Servers Reduces attack surface and malware exposure. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) Definition Access based on job responsibilities. Benefits • Reduced privilege • Better accountability • Easier auditing Just Enough Administration (JEA) Purpose Provide limited administrative capabilities using PowerShell. Benefits • Granular privileges • Reduced attack surface • Supports Zero Trust principles RDP Security Risks RDP exposed to the internet is a common attack vector. Recommendations • Block external RDP access • Use VPNs • Use RD Gateway • Restrict access via WFAS Security Point Changing the RDP port is obscurity, not security. Disabling Weak Encryption Protocols Deprecated Technologies • SSL 3.0 • TLS 1.0 Secure Alternatives • TLS 1.2 • TLS 1.3 Management Tools • Registry • IIS Crypto Security Principle Remove outdated cryptographic protocols to prevent exploitation. Chapter Takeaways Students should leave this chapter understanding that modern Windows security relies on multiple layers: Endpoint protection (Defender) Host firewalls (WFAS) Identity security (Entra Password Protection, LAPS) Encryption (BitLocker, IPsec) Detection and response (Defender for Endpoint, Defender for Identity) Administrative hardening (RBAC, JEA, least privilege) The overarching theme is Defense in Depth and Zero Trust, where no user, device, or network segment is inherently trusted and security controls must exist at every layer.

ict-218/security-concepts.html.description: Confidentiality ensures information is only accessible to authorized individuals. The goal is to prevent unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information.• Encryption • Access Control Lists (ACLs) • Data Classification • MFA • File PermissionsStudent Records Only instructors, advisors, and authorized staff should be able to view grades.Medical Records Only authorized medical personnel should access patient filesIntegrity ensures data remains accurate, complete, and unaltered. Users must trust that information has not been modified improperly.• Hashing • Digital Signatures • Checksums • Version Control • Database Constraints• Bank account balances • Student grades • Financial transactionsAvailability ensures systems and information remain accessible when needed.• Backups • Redundancy • Failover Systems • Disaster Recovery Plans • UPS Power Protection• Microsoft 365 services • Banking systems • Hospital information systemsNon-repudiation ensures a person cannot deny performing an action. It provides proof of: • Origin • Delivery • Identity • TransactionA cryptographic signature that proves: • Who sent the message • Message authenticity • Message integrityRecord: • Login attempts • File access • Administrative activitiesValidate identities in electronic communications.AAA is one of the most important access-control concepts in cybersecurity.Authentication verifies identity. Question: "Who are you?"Something You Know • Password • PIN Something You Have • Smartphone • Security Token Something You Are • Fingerprint • Face RecognitionAuthorization determines what users are allowed to do. Question: "What are you allowed to access?"A student can: • View grades A professor can: • View grades • Modify gradesAccounting records actions performed by users. Question: "What did the user do?"• Login history • File access logs • Administrative actions • Audit reportsZero Trust follows the principle: Never Trust, Always Verify No user, device, or application is automatically trusted, even if located inside the network.Traditional security assumes: Outside Network = Untrusted Inside Network = Trusted If attackers gain access internally, they can move laterally across systems. Everyone = Continuously Verified • Identity • Device Health • Location • Risk Score • User BehaviorThe Control Plane makes security decisions. It evaluates: • Policies • Risk • Identities • Threat IntelligenceThe Data Plane enforces decisions made by the Control Plane.• Allow access • Deny access • Restrict access

ict-225/day-one-and-two-225.html.description:
we work on the network side of things firewalls routers switches Authentication you are who you say you are Authorization what can you do what permissions you have Accounting Event logs Module Title: Understanding Defense Module Objective: Explain approaches to network security defense. Cybersecurity analysts must prepare for any type of attack. It is their job to secure the assets of the organization’s network. Data is the one asset that cannot be replaced, it is the hardest to put a price on. To do this, cybersecurity analysts must first identify: what is an asset - Anything of value to an organization that must be protected including servers, infrastructure devices, end devices, and the greatest asset, data. Vulnerabilities - A weakness in a system or its design that could be exploited by a threat actor. Threats - Any potential danger to an asset. • The collection of all the devices and information owned or managed by an organization are assets. • The assets constitute the attack surface that threat actors could target. • As an organization grows, so do its assets. Consider the number of assets a large organization would have to protect. • Asset management consists of inventorying all assets, and then developing and implementing policies and procedures to protect them. • Organizations need to identify where critical information assets are stored, and how access is gained to that information.• Asset classification assigns an organization’s resources into groups based on common characteristics. • The most critical information needs to receive the highest level of protection and may even require special handling. • A labeling system can be used to determine how valuable, how sensitive, and how critical the information is. • The steps for identifying and classifying assets are: Determine the proper asset identification category: Information assets Software assets Physical assets Services Establish asset accountability by identifying the owner of each information asset and each piece of software: Identify the owner for all information assets. Identify the owner for all application software. Determine the criteria for classification Confidentiality Value Time Access rights Destruction Implement a classification schema: Adopt a consistent way of identifying information to ensure uniform protection and easier monitoring. Asset standards identify specific hardware and software products used by an organization. When a failure occurs, prompt action helps to maintain both access and security. If an organization does not standardize its hardware selection, personnel may need to scramble to find a replacement component. Non-standard environments require more expertise to manage, and they increase the cost of maintenance contracts and inventory • Part of the cybersecurity specialists’ job is to manage information assets and related systems throughout that asset´s lifecycle. The stages of asset´s lifecycle are: Procurement - The organization purchases the assets based on the needs identified from data gathered to justify the purchase. The asset is added to the organization’s inventory. Deployment -The asset is assembled and inspected to check for defects or other problems. Staff perform tests and install tags or barcodes for tracking purposes. The asset moves from inventory to in-use. Utilization -This is the longest stage of the cycle. The asset’s performance is continuously checked. Upgrades, patch fixes, new license purchases, and compliance audits are all part of the utilization stage. Maintenance It helps to extend an asset’s productive life. Staff may modify or upgrade the asset. Disposal - At the end of the asset’s productive life, it must be disposed of. All data must be wiped from the asset. Disposal may include dismantling an asset for parts. Any parts that can cause an environmental hazard must be disposed of according to local guidelines. have multiple layers of security to get to the asset eg AAA firewall IPS (intrusion prevention system) Hardened devices content filtering this is the key idea

the idea is that a threat actor will try to attack individual leaves to get to the data/core asset. To make sure data and infrastructure remain secure, an organization should create different layers of protection: Layering: To make sure data and information remains available, an organization must set up different layers of protection, creating a barrier of multiple defenses that work together to prevent attacks. Limiting: Limiting access to data and information reduces the possibility of a security threat. An organization should restrict access so that each user only has the level of access required to do their job. Diversity: If all defense layers were the same, it would not be very difficult for cybercriminals to succeed in an attack. The layers must be different so that if one layer is penetrated, the same technique will not work on all the others which would compromise the whole system Obscurity: Obscuring information can also protect data and information. An organization should not reveal any information that cybercriminals can use to identify which Operating System (OS) a server is running, or the type or make of equipment or software it uses. Simplicity: Complexity does not necessarily guarantee security. If employees do not understand how to configure a solution properly, such as setting up their account using an unnecessarily complex process, this may make it just as easy for cybercriminals to compromise those systems. • They are the guidelines that are developed by an organization to govern its actions. • The policies define standards of correct behavior for the business and its employees. • If behavior that violates business policy (baseline) is detected on the network, it is possible that a security breach has occurred. An organization may have several guiding policies:
A comprehensive security policy has several benefits: Demonstrates an organization’s commitment to security Sets the rules for expected behavior Ensures consistency in system operations, software and hardware acquisition and use, and maintenance Defines the legal consequences of violations Gives security staff the backing of management Security policies are used to inform users, staff, and managers of an organization’s requirements for protecting technology and information assets. A security policy also specifies the mechanisms that are needed to meet security requirements and provides a baseline from which to acquire, configure, and audit computer systems and networks for compliance. Policies in a security policy may include:
Configuration includes all the settings that you configure for a system which provide the foundation for all similar systems - like a template of sorts normal operations so that if an irregular event does occur, it can be detected! Baselining data takes timeItem’s to build defenses around: Hardware OS Protocols Tracking events that occur on end and intermediary devices (Workstations, Servers, Switches, Routers, etc) Categories of Logs (ie for the os, Applications) Categories of Events - Severity Levels, etc

ict-225/hashing.html.description:
Integrity Checks (Cont.)How a checksum works:. A checksum verifies the integrity of files, or strings of characters, before and after they transfer
between devices across a local network or the Internet.
Checksums convert each piece of information to a value and sums the total.
To test the data integrity, a receiving system repeats the process. If the two sums are equal,
the data is valid. If not, a change has occurred somewhere along the line.Hash functions:. Common hash functions include MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256 and SHA-512.
. These use complex mathematical algorithms to compare data to a hashed value.

ict-225/high-availability.html.title: High Availability
ict-225/high-availability.html.icon: <svg class="svg-icon lucide-file" stroke-linejoin="round" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-width="2" stroke="currentColor" fill="none" viewBox="0 0 24 24" height="24" width="24" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M6 22a2 2 0 0 1-2-2V4a2 2 0 0 1 2-2h8a2.4 2.4 0 0 1 1.704.706l3.588 3.588A2.4 2.4 0 0 1 20 8v12a2 2 0 0 1-2 2z"></path><path d="M14 2v5a1 1 0 0 0 1 1h5"></path></svg>
ict-225/high-availability.html.description: The term 'high availability' describes systems designed to avoid downtime as much as possible. The continuous availability of information systems is imperative, not only to organizations but to modern life, as we are all using and relying on computer and information systems more than ever before. High availability systems typically are based on three design principles: eliminating single points of failure, providing for reliable crossover, and detecting failures as they occur. The first principle that defines high availability systems starts with identifying all system devices and components whose failure would result in system-wide failure. Methods to eliminate single points of failure include replacing or removing hot stand-by devices, redundant components, and multiple connections or pathways. Redundant power supplies, backup power systems and backup communications systems all provide for reliable crossover - the second design principle. The third principle is active device and system monitoring to detect many types of events including system and device failures. Monitoring systems may even trigger the backup system in the case of failure. Every organization wants to be able to operate uninterrupted, even under extreme conditions, such as during an attack.One of the most popular high availability goals is often called 'five nines.' It gets its name from its aim to achieve an availability rate of 99.999%, which is five nines in a row. In practice, this means that downtime is less than 5.26 minutes per year.Common steps taken to reach the five nines include: Standardized Systems Systems standardization provides for systems that use the same components. As a result, parts inventories are easier to maintain and it is possible and easy to swap components, even during an emergency. In highly secure information system facilities, guards control access to the organization's sensitive areas. The benefit of using guards here is that they can adapt more than automated systems. Guards can learn and distinguish many different conditions and situations and make decisions on the spot. Clustering Multiple devices grouped together provide a service that, to users, appears to be a single entity. If one device in a cluster fails, the other devices remain available and can step in. Shared Component Systems Systems are built so that a complete system can stand in for one that failed. N+1 redundancy helps ensure system availability in the event of a component failure. It means that components (N) need to have at least one backup component (+1). A good way to think about this is that a car has four tires (N) and a spare tire (+1) in the trunk in case of a flat. Although a system using N+1 architecture contains redundant equipment, it is not a fully redundant system. My summary Always have at least one extra of what you need always ready for the event that it goes down. N +1 Is specifically not in use/on its own. Like bellow the N+1 is the secondary network, not the redundancy in the first.

ict-225/network-hardening.html.description:
Dynamic host configuration protocol (DHCP) uses a server to assign an IP address and other configuration information to network devices. In effect, the device gets a permission slip from the DHCP server to use the network. Attackers can target DHCP servers to deny access to devices on the network, but security measures like DHCP snooping prevent rogue DHCP servers from providing IP addresses to clients by validating messages from sources that are not trusted.. A security checklist for DHCP: . Physically secure the DHCP server. . Apply any software patches. . Locate the DHCP server behind a firewall. . Monitor DHCP activity by reviewing DHCP logs. · Maintain a strong antivirus solution. . Uninstall any unused services and applications. .Close unused ports.recognize the IP address. |.Enable logging and analyze logs.Domain name system (DNS) translates a URL or website address, such as www.cisco.com, into a numerical IP address. When users type a web address into the address bar, the DNS server will IDNS Security Extensions (DNSSEC) uses digital signatures to strengthen authentication and protect against threats to the DNS.. A security checklist for DNS: . Keep DNS software up to date. . Prevent version string from revealing information. Separate internal and external DNS servers. Restrict allowed transactions by client IP address. Use transaction signatures to authenticate transactions. Disable or restrict zone transfers and dynamic updates as much as possible. . . . Use Domain Name System Security Extensions (DNSSEC). Sign zones.CISCOO 2020 Ciaco and/or its affilintos. All sights raserved. Cisco ConfidentialInternet control messaging protocol (ICMP): Network devices use ICMP to send error messages that a requested service is not available, or the host could not reach the router, for example.. The ping command is a network utility that uses ICMP to test the reachability of a host on a network. . Ping sends ICMP messages to the host and waits for a reply. . Cybercriminals can alter the use of ICMP to run reconnaissance, denial of service (DoS) and covert channel attacks. . Many networks filter ICMP requests to prevent such attacks.Routing information protocol: RIP is a routing protocol that limits the number of hops from source to destination that are allowed in a network path. . The maximum number of hops allowed for RIP is fifteen. . RIP is used to exchange routing information about which networks each router can reach and how far away those networks are.. RIP calculates the best route based on hop count, but cybercriminals can also target routers and the RIP protocol. . Such attacks on routing services can affect performance and availability, some attacks can even result in traffic redirection. . Use secure services with authentication and implement system patching and updates to protect routing services.Network Time Protocol (NTP) is a protocol that synchronizes network computer system clocks.Having the correct time within networks is important. . Correct timestamps accurately track network events such as security violations. . Additionally, clock synchronization is critical for the correct interpretation of events within syslog data files as well as for digital certificates.. NTP allows network devices to synchronize their time settings with an NTP server. . Cybercriminals attack timeservers to disrupt secure communication that depends on digital certificates and to hide attack information. . Use NTP Authentication to verify that the server is trusted.Telnet, SSH, and SCPSecure Shell (SSH) is a protocol that provides a secure (encrypted) remote connection to a device.Telnet is an older protocol that uses unsecure plaintext when authenticating a device (username and password) and transmitting data.. SSH should be used rather than Telnet to manage connections, as it provides strong encryption. SSH uses TCP port 22. Telnet uses TCP port 23.Secure copy (SCP) securely transfers files between two remote systems.. SCP uses SSH for data transfer and authentication, ensuring the authenticity and confidentiality of the data in transit.CISCOSecure ProtocolsAttackers can penetrate a network's infrastructure through services, protocols, and open ports.Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) collects statistics from TCP/IP devices to monitor network and computer equipment. SNMPv3 is the current standard - it uses cryptography to prevent eavesdropping and make sure data hasn't been tampered with while in transit.Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP) provides basic web connectivity and uses port 80. HTTP contains limited built-in security and is open to traffic monitoring when transmitting content, leaving the o user's computer open to attack.Protocols that provide a more secure connection: . Secure Sockets Layer (SSL) manages encryption by using an SSL handshake at the beginning of a session to provide confidentiality and prevent eavesdropping and tampering. . Transport Layer Security (TLS) is an updated, more secure replacement for SSL. SSL/TLS encrypts communication between the client and the server. Where it's used, the user will see HTTPS in the URL field of a browser instead of HTTP. 2020 Claco and/or its affiliates. All rights reserved. Cisco ConfidentialFile Transfer Protocol (FTP) transfers computer files between a client and a server. In FTP, the client uses a plaintext username and password to connect. File Transfer Protocol Secure (FTPS) is more secure - it adds support for TLS and SSL to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and forgery on exchanged messages.Email uses Post Office Protocol (POP), Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) and Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (MIME) to attach non-text data, such as an image or video, to an email message.. To secure POP (port 110) or IMAP (port 143), use SSL/TLS to encrypt mail during transmission. The Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) protocol provides a secure method of transmission. It sends digitally signed and encrypted messages that provide authentication, message integrity, and nonrepudiation.The network is segmented. . VLANs allow an administrator to segment a network based on factors such as function, project, team, or application. . Devices within a VLAN act as if they are in their own independent network, even though they share a common infrastructure with other VLANs on the same LAN. . A VLAN can separate groups of devices that host sensitive data from the rest of the network, decreasing the chances of confidential information breaches - in our example, the HR department looking to protect sensitive data. . Trunks allow individuals on the HR VLAN to be physically connected to multiple switches.Data is protected. . VLANs provide a way to limit broadcast traffic in a switched network. . To protect the VLAN, monitor its performance, use advanced configurations, and regularly install patches and updates.A demilitarized zone (DMZ) is a small network between a trusted private network and the Internet.Access to untrusted networks: Web servers and mail servers are usually placed within the DMZ to allow users to access an untrusted network, such as the Internet, without compromising the internal network.
Zero trust model: Firewalls manage east-west traffic (traffic that goes between servers within the organization's data center) and north-south traffic (data moving into and out of the organization's network).. To protect its network, an organization can implement a Zero Trust model. . Automatically trusting users and endpoints within the organization can put any network at risk, as trusted users can move throughout the network to access data. . Zero Trust networking constantly monitors all users on the network regardless of their status or role.

info_showOrphanNodes.description: Show nodes that are not connected to any other nodes.

info_showAttachments.description: Show attachments like images and PDFs as nodes in the graph.

info_allowGlobalGraph.description: Allow the user to view the global graph of all nodes.

info_allowExpand.description: Allow the user to pop-out the graph view to take up the whole screen

info_attractionForce.description: How much should linked nodes attract each other? This will make the graph appear more clustered.

info_linkLength.description: How long should the links between nodes be? The shorter the links the more connected nodes will cluster together.

info_repulsionForce.description: How much should nodes repel each other? This will make disconnected parts more spread out.

info_centralForce.description: How much should nodes be attracted to the center? This will make the graph appear more dense and circular.

info_edgePruning.description: Edges with a length above this threshold will not be rendered, however they will still contribute to the simulation. This can help large tangled graphs look more organised. Hovering over a node will still display these links.

info_minNodeRadius.description: How small should the smallest nodes be? The smaller a node is the less it will attract other nodes.

info_maxNodeRadius.description: How large should the largest nodes be? Nodes are sized by how many links they have. The larger a node is the more it will attract other nodes. This can be used to create a good grouping around the most important nodes.

info_allowResizing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be resized

info_allowCollapsing.description: Whether or not to allow the sidebars to be collapsed

info_rightDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the right sidebar

info_leftDefaultWidth.description: The default width of the left sidebar
